hits.title: ASTRONOMY — Of the Systems of the World
hits.snippet: The Ptolemaic system, which placed the earth immoveable in the centre, is now universally exploded; the Copernican, which places the sun in the centre, is demonstrated to be the true system of the world.

hits.title: ASTRONOMY — Of the Solar System
hits.snippet: The solar system consists of the sun, and the planets and comets moving about him. The planets are six in number: Mercury, Venus, the Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.

text:
Sir, the matter admits of no great dispute. **Astronomy** is the science which teaches the knowledge of the celestial bodies, their magnitudes, motions, distances, periods, eclipses, and order [EB:1771-v1-p487].

The solar system consists of the sun, with the planets and comets moving about him; and the primary planets are **six in number** — Mercury, Venus, the Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn [EB:1771-v1-p489]. The Ptolemaic system, which placed the earth immoveable in the centre, is now universally exploded; the Copernican system is demonstrated to be the true system of the world, displaying the wisdom and power of the Creator [EB:1771-v1-p491].

hits.title: Astronomy
hits.snippet: Astronomy is a natural science that studies celestial objects and the phenomena that occur in the cosmos. It uses mathematics, physics, and chemistry to explain their origin and their overall evolution.

text:
Some of that holds up well. Astronomy is still defined as the natural science that studies celestial objects and phenomena — now explicitly using mathematics, physics and chemistry [WP:Astronomy].

But the planet count is out of date: the Solar System has **eight planets**, adding Uranus and Neptune to your six [WP:Solar_System#planets]. Pluto was even counted as a ninth from 1930 until the IAU reclassified it as a **dwarf planet** in 2006 [WP:Pluto#classification].

hits.title: ASTRONOMY — Discovery of New Planets
hits.snippet: In 1781 Sir William Herschel discovered the planet Uranus; and in 1846 the planet Neptune was found in the place assigned to it by the calculations of Le Verrier and Adams.

text:
I grant the point with pleasure, for our own later editions record it. In 1781 Sir William Herschel discovered the planet Uranus, and in 1846 Neptune was found in the very place assigned to it by the calculations of Le Verrier and Adams [EB:1853-v4-p12] — the most signal triumph of physical astronomy.

Yet I would remind my learned friend that the planets are, in all probability, inhabited like our earth [EB:1771-v1-p489], and that the *plurality of worlds* was affirmed by the best philosophers of the age [EB:1771-v3-p118].

hits.title: Heliocentrism
hits.snippet: Heliocentrism is a superseded astronomical model in which the Earth and planets revolve around the Sun at the center of the universe. Copernicus presented the mathematical model in 1543.

text:
Agreed on Herschel and Le Verrier — the modern record matches yours almost word for word [WP:Solar_System#planets].

On the Sun-centred system we also agree, though the framing differs: today heliocentrism is described as a *superseded* model — the Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars with no special place in the universe, and no appeal is made to a Creator [WP:Heliocentrism]. As for inhabited planets, the modern articles make no such claim; there is simply no counterpart to that statement.

summary: The two encyclopaedias agree on what astronomy is and that the planets circle the Sun, but 250 years of discovery separate them on the contents of the solar system: Uranus, Neptune and the dwarf planets did not exist for the 1771 reader. The deepest shift is in perspective — the 18th-century text reads the heavens as evidence of a Creator and speculates about inhabited worlds, claims with no modern counterpart.
